title: Creating Files and Folders
objective: Learn to create empty files with touch and new directories with mkdir, including nested directories.
explanation: Now that you know how to move around the filesystem, it is time to start creating things. In Linux, you create empty files with the touch command and new folders (directories) with mkdir. The touch command is simple: type touch followed by a file name, and Linux creates an empty file with that name. If the file already exists, touch does not erase it — it just updates the timestamp to the current time. That is actually what touch was originally designed for, but most people use it to quickly create new files. You can create multiple files at once by listing them: touch file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt. To create a directory, use mkdir (short for make directory). Type mkdir followed by the folder name: mkdir projects creates a new folder called projects. Just like touch, you can create multiple directories at once: mkdir photos videos games. But what if you want to create a folder inside a folder that does not exist yet? For example, you want to create projects/python/games but neither projects nor python exist. If you try mkdir projects/python/games, Linux will complain because it cannot create games inside python if python does not exist yet. The solution is the -p flag, which stands for parents. When you type mkdir -p projects/python/games, Linux creates all the missing directories in the path. It builds the whole chain for you. This is one of the most useful flags in Linux. File names in Linux are case-sensitive. That means Report.txt and report.txt are two completely different files. Also, avoid spaces in file names when possible. If you must use a space, put quotes around the name: touch "my file.txt". But most Linux users prefer dashes or underscores: my-file.txt or my_file.txt.

challenge.question: Create a directory structure for a school project: school/science/experiments with a file called hypothesis.txt inside experiments. What commands do you need?
challenge.hint: Use mkdir -p to create the nested folders, then touch to create the file inside.

funFact: The touch command is named after the idea of touching a file to update its timestamp. It is like tapping a document to mark it as recently accessed, even if you did not change anything inside!
